metaDescription: Five cordless impact drivers under $100 compared on peak torque claims, impacts per minute, brushless motors and whether a battery is included.
expertTake: Under $100 you can buy a genuine impact driver from a name brand, and that is the smart route if you drive deck screws or lag bolts. The DEWALT DCF787D1 is the best overall because it adds a brushless motor and a real platform to a kit that includes a battery. The Ryobi is the value pick if you already own ONE+ batteries, and the Litheli is the cheapest way to get a working kit. Skip this price tier if you want to loosen rusted bolts, because an impact driver is for fastening, not breaking free seized hardware.
introParagraphs: An impact driver hammers sideways as it spins, which lets a small tool drive long screws that would stall a drill. That mechanism is also why the torque numbers on budget listings are so confusing, since many quote the force of the hammer blow or the stall point rather than anything you can feel in the work.

This guide explains what an impact driver gives up when the price falls under a hundred dollars, which claims to ignore and which kits are worth owning. The quick picks are above, and the reviews below match each driver to the kind of fastening it handles best.

products.name: DEWALT 20V MAX DCF787D1 Brushless 1/4-Inch Impact Driver Kit

specList.label: Work light
specList.value: LED with 20 second delay after release

products.description:
The DCF787D1 is the cheapest way to get a brushless impact driver on a major platform. Brushless means the controller switches the motor current electronically instead of through carbon brushes, so the driver wastes less energy as heat and runs longer on a pack. In impact work that efficiency is visible on the third bag of screws.

It carries no headline torque number on this listing, which is unusual and actually refreshing next to drivers advertising 1,500 or more inch-pounds. The Litheli claims 1,593 in-lbs and the Craftsman 1,460, but those are peak figures that do not equal real fastening torque. A name-brand driver is rated through a consistent test and sold by a company that will answer a warranty claim.

The larger benefit is the platform. A 20V MAX kit lets you add bare tools later, such as a drill driver or circular saw, without buying another battery, which makes this the sensible start of a cordless collection. The LED stays on for 20 seconds after you release the trigger so you can check the fastener.

Battery and charger included in the kit

LED holds for 20 seconds after you release the trigger

products.badge: Best Value if You Own ONE+
products.name: RYOBI ONE+ 18V 1/4-Inch Impact Driver, 1,800 in-lbs, Tool Only
products.description:
The Ryobi is sold bare, so its low price depends on you owning a ONE+ battery already. If you do, it is the strongest value in this guide: 1,800 inch-pounds of claimed torque and 0-3,400 impacts per minute, the highest impact rate here. Impacts per minute describe how many times the hammer mechanism strikes the anvil, and a higher rate gives a smoother feel in thick lumber.

If you do not own a battery, the math flips. A battery and charger are a significant extra cost, so compare the all-in total against the DEWALT and Craftsman kits. The torque claim of 1,800 is the highest on the page, but as with every no-load or peak figure it does not predict how it fastens a lag bolt.

ONE+ is a sprawling system with tools for lawn, garage and car, and the same pack fits all of them. The chuck accepts standard 1/4-inch hex bits and drops them one-handed. Keep the pack off the charger once full and avoid leaving the driver in a hot car, which is the fastest way to age a lithium cell.
products.bestFor: Ryobi owners and buyers who want to build around a large affordable platform.
pros: Highest claimed torque and impact rate in the group
Huge ONE+ platform of tools shares the same battery
One-handed quick-release chuck for fast bit changes
Bare tool saves money for existing Ryobi owners
cons: No battery or charger included in the box
Peak torque figure overstates real fastening force
All-in cost rises if you start without a pack

products.name: CRAFTSMAN 20V MAX CMCF800C1 Impact Driver Kit, 2,800 RPM
products.description:
The CMCF800C1 is the plain, honest kit of the group, publishing torque, speed and impact rate, which makes comparison possible. At 1,460 in-lbs, 2,800 rpm and 3,100 IPM it gives up about 340 in-lbs of claimed torque and 300 impacts per minute to the Ryobi, but you get a battery and charger in the box. That is the real reason to choose it.

The maximum speed of 2,800 rpm is lower than the B+D's 3,000, and that is fine because impact drivers are slowed by the hammer anyway. A lower top rpm gives somewhat finer trigger control when starting a screw. The listing does not mention a brushless motor, which is the main way it differs from the DEWALT and a reason it costs less.

The Craftsman V20 platform shares batteries with a range of other tools, which helps if you later expand. Expect it to be noisier than a drill because the hammer mechanism cracks as it engages, so wear hearing protection for long sessions. Check that the bit is seated fully in the quick-release chuck before pulling the trigger.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want a complete kit from an established brand without paying for brushless.
pros: Publishes torque, rpm and impact rate for fair comparison
Includes battery and charger for immediate use
Quick-release chuck allows one-handed bit changes
Platform shared with other Craftsman V20 tools
cons: Not listed as brushless like the DEWALT
Lower claimed torque than the Ryobi and Litheli
Single battery limits long fastening sessions

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 20V MAX POWERCONNECT BDCI20C Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
The BDCI20C posts the highest impact rate on paper, 3,900 impacts per minute, and the lowest torque, 1,375 in-lbs. Those two numbers describe a driver tuned for lots of quick, light impacts rather than a few heavy ones. It suits hanging shelves, assembling raised beds and driving short exterior screws into softwood.

Its price positions it near the bottom of the name-brand range, and the kit includes a battery and charger. Compared with the Craftsman, which gives you 85 more inch-pounds and a similar kit, the B+D trades power for a wider platform of cheap home-oriented tools. The POWERCONNECT batteries fit an extensive set of mowers, trimmers and vacuums.

The weakness is stamina on large work. A smaller transmission and a basic motor will strain with 3-inch structural screws into hardwood, and you will notice the pack running down. For weekend projects it is perfectly adequate, and the body's light weight reduces forearm fatigue.
products.bestFor: Occasional DIYers who want a light, low-cost impact driver from a familiar brand.
pros: Highest impact rate in this roundup at 3,900 IPM
Light body reduces fatigue on overhead screws
POWERCONNECT battery fits many B+D home tools
Complete kit with battery and charger
cons: Lowest claimed torque among the name-brand kits
Basic motor strains on long structural screws
Platform tools skew toward light home use

products.name: Litheli 20V Cordless Impact Driver Kit, 2.0Ah, 1593 in-lbs
products.description:
The Litheli is the cheapest working kit in the group and the only budget pick with a 2.0 Ah battery alongside a published torque claim of 1,593 inch-pounds. It reaches 3,000 impacts per minute, which is competitive. The listing promotes stable output rather than inflated numbers, which is reasonable, though no peak figure on any listing can be verified from the page alone.

Against the Craftsman it offers about 130 more inch-pounds of claimed torque at a lower position in the price range, but it lacks the name-brand warranty and a deep platform. A tool from a lesser-known maker may have fewer service options and fewer replacement batteries. If the battery fails after two years, you may be buying a new kit rather than a replacement.

It is the sensible choice if you only need an impact driver for a few projects and want to minimize spend. The compact body is shaped for overhead and tight work, and the angled LED reduces the shadow cast by the bit. Do not expect it to outlast a DEWALT through daily use.
products.bestFor: Budget-first buyers who need a working kit for a few projects.
pros: Lowest price among the kits that include a battery
2.0 Ah battery is larger than most budget packs

buyingCriteria.explanation: A brushless motor uses electronic switching instead of carbon brushes, so it runs cooler and wastes less energy. Among these picks only the DEWALT DCF787D1 is listed as brushless, and that is the feature that justifies a higher price. Drivers whose listings do not say brushless, such as the Craftsman CMCF800C1 and BLACK+DECKER BDCI20C, still work but typically run down packs faster. For a driver you use weekly, brushless pays back. A good habit is to test any new impact driver on a scrap board with a 3-inch screw and listen for the hammer engaging, since a driver that never seems to hammer is under-torqued for the job.

Listings advertise numbers like the Ryobi's 1,800 in-lbs and Litheli's 1,593 in-lbs, which are generally peak or stall values. Real fastening torque, the twist that drives a lag screw home, is lower. Two drivers with similar claims can feel very different, so use claims only to rank within a brand and prefer drivers that publish rpm and impacts per minute. Sit the claimed figures side by side before shopping: the Ryobi at 1,800, the Litheli at 1,593, the Craftsman at 1,460 and the BLACK+DECKER at 1,375 in-lbs span about 425 inch-pounds on paper.

IPM counts how often the hammer strikes the anvil. The BDCI20C reaches 3,900, the Ryobi 3,400, the Craftsman 3,100 and the Litheli 3,000. A higher rate delivers smaller, more frequent blows that feel smoother, while a lower rate with heavier blows feels harsher. Do not read IPM as power, since torque per blow matters as much. On a day of driving 3-inch screws, the DEWALT's brushless motor should keep the pack from heating as quickly as the conventional motors in the Craftsman and BLACK+DECKER kits.

The Ryobi ships bare, while the DEWALT, Craftsman, BLACK+DECKER and Litheli include a battery and charger. A bare tool looks cheaper but is only good value if you already own the pack. Add the cost of a battery before comparing, and note that one battery in a kit means you wait for the charger on long jobs. A kit battery of about 2.0 Ah is typical here, and that is roughly an hour of intermittent fastening before you need to wait for the charger.

Within a few years you will want a drill, saw or light on the same battery. The DEWALT 20V MAX, Craftsman V20, Ryobi ONE+ and BLACK+DECKER POWERCONNECT each have large lineups, while the Litheli does not. A cheap driver on an orphan platform loses its value when the pack dies. The BLACK+DECKER and Ryobi platforms are strong on home and garden tools, while the DEWALT platform leans toward job-site tools.

These drivers accept only 1/4-inch hex bits, and the hammer action makes them poor for fine drilling or any job that needs a clutch. They excel at driving long screws without stripping. If you want one cordless tool, a drill driver is the more flexible choice, and the impact driver is the second tool. If you want one cordless tool and plan to drill holes, buy a drill driver first, and add the impact driver when you start driving long screws.

specDecoder.meaning: Inch-pounds measure rotational force, and for impact drivers manufacturers usually quote the peak, produced by the hammer blow or at stall.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Litheli's 1,593 and Ryobi's 1,800 in-lbs are not directly comparable with the DEWALT, which publishes no figure.

specDecoder.meaning: This counts hammer strikes per minute. Each strike adds a short burst of torque, which is why an impact driver can drive a screw a drill would stall on.
specDecoder.watchFor: A high IPM like the BDCI20C's 3,900 does not mean more power, only more frequent blows.

specDecoder.meaning: A brushless motor uses electronic commutation and permanent magnets, with no brushes to wear out. It is more efficient and holds up better under load.
specDecoder.watchFor: Verify the listing says brushless. Among the lineup only the DEWALT does, so treat the others as conventional.

specDecoder.meaning: 20V MAX is the peak voltage of a fresh pack, while the nominal voltage is 18V. The Ryobi's 18V rating and DEWALT's 20V MAX are the same class.
specDecoder.watchFor: Voltage names are marketing. Pack capacity and motor design matter more.

specDecoder.meaning: The chuck is a hex socket that accepts bits with a hex shank. It locks bits in place and lets you swap them with one hand.
specDecoder.watchFor: Standard round-shank drill bits will not fit without an adapter.

howWeEvaluated.title: Torque in context
howWeEvaluated.description: We listed each claimed torque figure and treated it as a peak value. The Ryobi (1,800), Litheli (1,593), Craftsman (1,460) and BLACK+DECKER (1,375) were compared only as a rough ranking. The DEWALT, which publishes none, was ranked on design.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor type
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored designs listed as brushless for efficiency and durability, since a brushless driver runs longer per charge and wears less. The DEWALT was the clear outlier.

howWeEvaluated.title: What is in the box
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted whether each listing includes a battery and charger, because the cost of a missing pack can erase a low price. The Ryobi's bare-tool format was handled separately.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform depth
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how many other tools share each battery, since a driver that sits on a large platform is easier to expand and replace.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit across the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: We then placed each driver by owner type, from the Litheli for minimal spend to the DEWALT for the longest-lived tool.

maintenance.why: Packed vents cause overheating. Compressed air keeps the airflow clear.
A worn bit cams out and damages screw heads. Impact-rated bits last longer.
Dirt can stop bits from locking. Clean and lightly oil the collar.
Heat ages lithium cells. Avoid cars and sheds in summer.
A worn anvil lets bits wobble. Replace it if the bit rocks in the socket.

faq.q: Is an impact driver worth it under $100?
faq.a: Yes, if you drive long screws. The hammer action prevents stalling and reduces wrist twist. For occasional light screws, a drill is enough. A drill driver is the more flexible first tool, and the impact driver is the second.

faq.q: Do I need brushless at this price?
faq.a: Brushless gives longer run time and lifespan, but costs more. Casual users can save money with a brushed model. If you are unsure, buy the brushless DEWALT kit, because it is the one you will not outgrow quickly.

faq.q: Can an impact driver replace a drill?
faq.a: Not entirely. It accepts only hex bits and has no clutch, so it is poor for precise drilling or delicate screws. They are not designed to drill holes, but with a hex-shank bit they can make small pilot holes.

faq.q: Why are claimed torque numbers so high?
faq.a: They are usually peak values at stall or at the hammer blow. Real fastening torque is lower, so use them only as a rough guide.

faq.q: Should I buy a tool-only impact driver?
faq.a: Only if you already own a compatible battery. Otherwise a kit is better value.
Yes. The hammer cracks as it engages, so wear hearing protection for long jobs.
